**Build automation with your AI agent. See exactly what will run.**

Open Flow is a source-available workflow platform for people who want the speed of AI-assisted building
and the clarity of a visual workflow. Ask Codex, Claude Code, or another agent to build a Flow, open
it in the Workbench, and keep refining the same workflow together.

Combine JavaScript, connected apps, AI, branching, and human approval in one canvas. Inspect the
inputs, follow the execution, and decide which version goes live. Run on OOMOL Hosted or on your
own infrastructure.

[Explore the interactive demo](https://openflow.run) · [Use OOMOL Hosted](https://console.openflow.run) ·
[Self-host with Docker](#run-it-your-way)

A vertical AI trend workflow in the Open Flow Workbench, with parallel X, GitHub, and Hugging Face sources and the Research & write node's prompt, tools, inputs, and output in the property panel

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Open Flow is in beta. The product and its versioned contracts are still evolving.

## Your agent builds. You stay in control.

Describe the work you need done:

> “Read new support emails, classify each request, draft a reply, and ask me to approve it before
> sending.”

Through [`oo flow`](https://github.com/oomol-lab/oo-cli), a terminal agent can discover integrations,
create and edit nodes, check a draft, run it, inspect results, and publish when you ask. Its changes
appear in the same Workbench you use to review the graph and edit the code. There is no separate
AI-generated project to translate or keep in sync.

The Server also exposes [MCP authoring and run tools](docs/server/mcp.md) for compatible clients.
Both interfaces work against the selected deployment's saved Flows, revisions, and runs.

Use an agent for the repetitive wiring. Keep the decisions that matter visible.

## Put every step where you can inspect it

A workflow should still make sense after the conversation that created it is gone.

- **JavaScript for precise work.** Transform data, format messages, or write custom logic in Code
  Tasks with named, typed inputs and outputs.
- **Explicit input sources.** See where a value comes from in the property panel. Control
  connections determine what executes next; input mappings determine what data a step receives.
- **Branches and reusable subflows.** Route work with conditions and give repeated logic a clear
  interface of its own.
- **Notes alongside the work.** Explain a decision directly on the canvas so the next person can
  understand the intent.

The current Code Task property panel showing JavaScript, a customer input source, and a typed message output

## Give AI a job with boundaries

Use LLM Tasks to classify, extract, or summarize. Use Agent Tasks when a job needs several tool
calls. Surround them with ordinary code, conditions, and approvals where you need predictable
behavior.

An Agent Task has a configured model, declared tools, and execution limits. Its tool configuration
specifies the actions, accounts, and approval policy available to the model. You can require human
approval for a tool call, or place an Approval node in the workflow before the next step proceeds.

Approval and Wait nodes persist their waiting state. Work can resume after a decision without
replaying the steps already completed in that run.

## See what happened. Choose what goes live.

Test a draft from a chosen trigger and follow its execution in the Workbench. Inspect node results,
logs, errors, and pending approvals instead of reconstructing a run from the final message alone.
Run history keeps the execution tied to the revision that produced it.

An onboarding test run paused for human approval in the Open Flow Workbench

Publishing creates a versioned snapshot for Live automation. Continue editing the draft while the
published version runs, inspect earlier Publications, and roll back when needed.

Start work manually, on a schedule, through a webhook, or from supported provider events and
polling sources. The same deployment owns the workflow, its Live version, and its execution state.

## Connect apps without putting credentials in the graph

Open Flow uses a Connector runtime such as
[OpenConnector](https://github.com/oomol-lab/open-connector) to discover and execute actions for
services including Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion. Account credentials stay with the Connector;
workflows refer to Connection identities.

OOMOL Hosted provides managed OAuth apps for supported integrations. With a self-hosted stack,
you choose the Connector deployment and manage the required provider configuration and account
authorizations. Workflow logic and account access remain separate concerns.

See [Open Flow with OpenConnector and the oo CLI](docs/server/self-hosted-stack/README.md) for a
complete setup, including authorizing an account and building a first Flow.

## Run it your way

| Option           | What you manage                                                                      | Get started                                      |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| **OOMOL Hosted** | Your workflows and connected accounts; OOMOL operates the deployment.                | [Open OOMOL](https://console.openflow.run)       |
| **Docker**       | Your deployment, storage, backups, upgrades, and integrations.                       | Commands below                                   |
| **Fly.io**       | Your app, persistent volume, secrets, backups, and upgrades on Fly's infrastructure. | [Deployment guide](docs/server/fly-io/README.md) |

For a local self-hosted instance, install Docker and OpenSSL, then run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/oomol-lab/open-flow.git
cd open-flow

export OPEN_FLOW_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
docker build --file apps/server/Dockerfile --tag open-flow-server:dev .
docker run --rm \
  --publish 3000:3000 \
  --env OPEN_FLOW_TOKEN="$OPEN_FLOW_TOKEN" \
  --volume open-flow-data:/data/open-flow \
  open-flow-server:dev
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:3000](http://127.0.0.1:3000) and sign in with `OPEN_FLOW_TOKEN`. Flows and run
history are stored in the Docker volume. The operator token also authenticates CLI and API access.

Prefer a prebuilt image? Follow the [GHCR image guide](docs/server/docker-ghcr/README.md) and select
an explicit release tag during beta. The `latest` tag is reserved for stable releases.

Connector actions and LLM Tasks need their corresponding services configured. The Server does not
silently fall back to another provider. Before exposing a deployment publicly, follow the
[deployment guide](docs/server/container-delivery.md) and
[hardening checklist](SECURITY.md#hardening-your-deployment).

## Build on Open Flow

Open Flow uses the Open Flow License, based on Apache-2.0 with additional conditions. The repository includes the workflow contracts and runtime,
Workbench, CLI command package, and self-hosted Server. The versioned Control API keeps clients
independent of the deployment's storage and execution implementation.

Use the versions of Bun and Node.js pinned in `.bun-version` and `.node-version`:

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run dev
```

The development Workbench opens at [http://localhost:5174](http://localhost:5174). The first run
creates an operator token in `apps/server/.open-flow-dev/operator-token`. See
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for configuration, checks, and the component Lab.

agentes.chat

  The open-source, self-hosted Slack alternative where your team and AI agents work together.

   Website  ·
   Cloud  ·
   Self-hosting  ·
   Features  ·
   Discussions

Agents join your channels and DMs with a role, an owner and a budget, work where everyone can see,
and ask before anything sensitive. They think with Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, Gemini, Grok or any
OpenRouter model, use MCP tools, and get a computer and a browser of their own. Self-hosting is
free and always will be (AGPL-3.0, no license key), or use agentes.chat Cloud, the paid, hosted
option: both run this same codebase. Changing it without publishing your changes, or reselling it
under your own brand? There is a [commercial license](COMMERCIAL.md).

## Why agentes.chat

- **One conversation for people and agents.** Agents are members of the workspace, not a sidebar
  bot: they read the channel, answer when it's theirs to answer, and hand work back and forth.
- **Safe by default.** Merges, deploys and anything a connector marks sensitive wait for a person's
  approval in the chat. Every model call is budgeted and recorded per agent.
- **Agents that actually do the work.** Their own computer, a real browser you can watch and take
  over, Claude Code and Codex, routines on a schedule or an event, memory that learns.
- **Yours to run.** One command on a Linux server, Postgres as the only dependency, web, desktop and
  phone apps that connect to your server.

An open-source alternative to team chat with bolted-on AI bots, and to single-player agent apps such
as Grok Bot, ChatGPT dots, OpenBot.run and OpenMausBot (all of which it imports from).

## Quick start

- **Cloud:** sign up at [agentes.chat](https://agentes.chat).
- **Your own server** (Linux):

  ```sh
  curl -fsSL https://agentes.chat/install | sh
  ```

  It installs what's missing (Docker, after asking), and puts agentes.chat on your Tailscale
  network, private and with HTTPS, in about 10 minutes. [SELF_HOSTING.md](SELF_HOSTING.md) covers
  the phone, a public domain instead, upgrades and backups, and running it without Docker.

Each organization adds its own model key (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Z.ai, MiniMax, Command Code or
OpenRouter) in the app.

## Features

| Feature | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channels, threads and DMs | ✅ | Public and private channels, DMs with people and agents, and threads started from a message or a stretch of conversation, then followed, closed and archived. |
| Agents | ✅ | Each has a role, instructions, a model (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Z.ai, MiniMax, Command Code, or any of OpenRouter's), a monthly budget checked before every call, and an owner who gets its approvals and budget alerts. |
| Router | ✅ | A message nobody @mentioned goes to the router. Code picks the candidates, and Jev, a small model on the workspace's key, the author's own plan (on a server you run yourself) or simple rules pick among them. Up to four agents answer, or none, and the message says who picked. It never grants a permission. |
| Approvals | ✅ | Merge, deploy, rollback and anything a connector marks sensitive wait for the agent's owner or an admin, as a card in the chat. The approved action runs once, exactly as approved. |
| Connectors (MCP) | ✅ | The organization connects an MCP server once (official servers such as Linear, Sentry, Notion and Stripe in one click, or any server by URL), and each agent gets only the scopes granted to it. With a Composio key, Google Drive, Calendar, Sheets and Docs, Slack, Microsoft Teams, OneDrive, HubSpot, Salesforce, Zendesk, Asana, Figma, Intercom, Dropbox, Square, Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube, Pinterest, Reddit and WhatsApp Business connect through Composio. |
| Skills | ✅ | Markdown skills (`SKILL.md`) from a zip, a GitHub link or the editor, with versions. Agents load one when a task needs it. |
| Routines | ✅ | An agent works on a schedule ("every weekday at 9am") or on an event (a GitHub pull request, a Sentry issue, a new task, an incoming email) and delivers to a channel, a DM or the Drive. |
| Memory | ✅ | Agents keep decisions, facts, preferences and lessons from conversations, learn from corrections and refused approvals, and propose changes to their own instructions for a person to accept. |
| Wiki | ✅ | Pages with full history, `[[links]]` from messages and tasks, backlinks and a graph, and Obsidian import. Agents read it, and write only when a person asks. |
| Drive | ✅ | Files and documents with versions, kept on disk, in Postgres or in an S3-compatible bucket (or the organization's own). Documents export to Word and PDF. |
| Tasks | ✅ | A board with your own columns. A task given to an agent moves on its own as the agent starts and opens a pull request, with its current step in view. |
| Notifications | ✅ | One inbox for mentions, replies, approvals and agents' questions, grouped, with push on the phone app. |
| Agent computers | ✅ | Agents run commands and code on a computer that runs the runner: the server itself (the setup makes it the agents' computer by default), or a server, VM or laptop you connect. On agentes.chat Cloud, each workspace gets a computer of its own. |
| Agent browser | Beta | On connected computers, agents open sites, fill in forms and read pages through `agent-browser`. Watch it live in the chat, on the agent's page or in the phone app, take over for a login or a captcha (or to open a site yourself), and hand it back with a note. |
| Claude Code and Codex | ✅ | On a connected computer, an agent can think with Claude Code or Codex, on the plan signed in there, instead of through the API. Codex is still in testing. |
| Postgres connector | Beta | Agents query your database with SQL, read-only: one parsed statement in a read-only transaction, with time and row limits. |
| Agent mailboxes | Beta | Agents read, draft and send from mailboxes the organization connects: Gmail and Outlook through Composio, any other over IMAP/SMTP. Sending asks for approval by default. |
| Phone app | Beta | iPhone and Android (Expo), on agentes.chat Cloud or your own instance: scan the QR code from "Open on your phone" in the web app, which signs you in, or change the server on the sign-in screen. |
| Desktop app (macOS; Windows and Linux on x64 and ARM64) | Beta | agentes.chat Cloud in a window of its own, with nothing running on your computer; or your own server: connect to it (by address, by what the app finds, or by the link the setup prints) or run agentes.chat on this computer with no Docker (Mac and Linux). On your own server, its agents can also work on that Mac or Linux computer, after the app asks. Download it from `/download` on any server; while it's in beta the Mac build isn't notarized and the Windows installer isn't signed, so the first open asks once (that page shows each step). |
| Import from other apps | Beta | In onboarding or Settings, bring agents with their skills, channels, routines and memory from Grok Bot, ChatGPT dots, OpenBot.run, OpenMausBot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Paperclip or another agentes.chat workspace. Grok Bot, ChatGPT dots and any other app answer an export prompt. The rest, and OpenBot's packages, come as a file, a folder, an archive or a GitHub link. A preview comes first: skills arrive on, routines active, and keys never. A workspace exports as one file. |
| 14 languages | ✅ | The whole app in English, Brazilian Portuguese, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Russian, Turkish, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese and Indonesian. |
| Self-host (Docker) | ✅ | One command (`curl -fsSL https://agentes.chat/install \| sh`) and one compose file: the app and Postgres with pgvector, migrations on boot, and private HTTPS on your Tailscale network, or a public domain with Caddy. |
| Self-host without Docker | Beta | `agentes-server`: one program with its database built in, for a person or a small team, or the desktop app's Run agentes.chat on this computer. |

Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) explains how to
run it from source and the checks a change needs. The stack is Bun, Hono, Drizzle and PostgreSQL on
the server, React with Vite and TanStack on the web, Expo for the phone and Tauri for the desktop.

# 🧊 Dynamo for Revit 2026: Standalone Offline Build for Windows 11

## 📦 Intro

This repository distributes a standalone offline Windows x64 build of Dynamo for Revit, packaged for the Dynamo for Revit visual programming workflow on Windows 10 and 11. It is a self-contained setup assembled by independent maintainers and shipped as a versioned distribution package, not as an upstream vendor release. The bundle is intended for anyone who needs a working node-based scripting environment installed from local media without depending on a live vendor channel.

Offline deployment matters in environments where workstations are air-gapped, where bandwidth is constrained, or where reproducibility across a fleet of machines is a hard requirement. This distribution exists to make those deploys boring: one artifact, one hash, one documented layout on disk. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or derived from any upstream vendor release process.

The build targets the desktop scripting workspace surface and lands in both portable and installed modes from a single package. A single Dynamo for Revit on Windows deployment covers the graph editor, the package library, and the bundled runtime without requiring additional downloads after setup.

## 01 · ⬇️ Download

## 02 · ✨ Features

**🧊 Node Graph Editor**

Visual scripting surface with live preview, undo history, and graph-level documentation nodes.

**📦 Bundled Package Library**

Ships with the core node collection and a local package cache for offline graph loading.

**💾 Portable Mode**

Runs from a user-writable folder without touching system directories or shared registries.

**🔐 SHA256 Manifest**

Every release publishes a hash manifest so deployments can verify the artifact before install.

**🌐 Multilingual UI**

Interface strings for 12 or more locales, selectable at first-run initialization.

**⚙️ Reproducible Install**

Versioned installer path with preserved user state on upgrade, no separate updater service.

## 03 · ⚙️ How it works

The installer expands the application into a versioned program directory and seeds a per-user configuration folder in the Windows profile. It writes a package manifest alongside the binaries so later verification and cleanup can be scripted. No files land in system directories under the default path.

On first launch the build registers its file associations for graph files and writes default preference files under the user profile. It reads environment variables on startup to determine the plugin search path and the local package cache location. Initialization is idempotent, so a reinstall over the same version does not duplicate state.

Day to day the build runs entirely on the local host, with no network calls required for editing or graph execution. Updates are handled by running a newer versioned installer over the existing install, which migrates preferences and leaves user graphs in place. There is no background daemon and no scheduled task.

Integration is limited to what the user grants: shell file associations, an optional Start Menu shortcut, and an entry in the Windows installed-apps list. It coexists with other installations of the same application as long as the portable variant is not launched simultaneously from the same directory. External dependencies are limited to the bundled runtime, which is self-contained.

## 04 · 🧩 Compatibility

The build supports Windows 10 and Windows 11 on x64 hardware. Both the current Windows 11 feature update channel and the latest Windows 10 servicing channel are tested. 32-bit Windows and older releases are not supported targets.

PowerShell 5.1 is sufficient for the basic install and uninstall flows. PowerShell 7 and later is preferred for the hash verification and rollback helpers that ship alongside the release notes.

Comfortable on a recent x64 workstation with a modern multi-core CPU and standard system RAM for a desktop scripting tool. Disk footprint is modest by desktop application standards but expands with the user package library over time.

Coexistence is handled by keeping versioned program directories separate and letting the user pick the active version at launch. Portable mode does not touch the registry and does not claim file associations unless explicitly requested. Installed mode coordinates with Windows so that only one installation owns graph file associations at a time.

## 05 · 🔧 Requirements

| Component | Supported | Preferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OS | Windows 10 | Windows 11 |
| Shell | PowerShell 5.1+ | PowerShell 7+ |
| Network | Required to download | Stable broadband |
| Privileges | Standard user access | Standard user access |

## 06 · ❓ FAQ

### 🔒 Is this standalone build safe to install on Windows?

> [!CAUTION]
> On first run, Windows SmartScreen may warn for unsigned installers. Click **More info**, then **Run anyway** to continue. The build is an offline setup file; keep your antivirus enabled as usual.

### 🪟 Which Windows versions does the build support?

> [!NOTE]
> The build runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11 on x64. Older Windows releases and 32-bit targets are not supported.

### 📡 Can I use the build offline?

> [!TIP]
> Yes. After install, the build runs without a network connection. Only the initial retrieval step needs internet access.

### 🔄 How do updates work?

> [!NOTE]
> Updates ship as a newer versioned installer; running it over the existing install preserves your projects, templates, and preferences. No separate updater service is required.

### 🗑️ How do I uninstall it on Windows?

> [!WARNING]
> Open Settings, then Apps, then Installed apps, find the entry in the list, and choose Uninstall. Personal project files remain on disk unless you remove them manually.

### ⚙️ What are the technical specifications?

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - **System load:** Light for graph editing, moderate for large package library scans on first open.
> - **File formats:** Reads and writes `.dyn` graphs and imports `.json` package manifests.
> - **Portable build:** A portable variant is included in the same release as the installed build.

### 🔐 How do I verify the file with SHA256?

> [!CAUTION]
> Open PowerShell in the folder with the installer and run `Get-FileHash setup.exe -Algorithm SHA256`. Compare the output with the hash published alongside the release. If they do not match, delete the file and fetch it again.

### 🛡️ Does the build require administrator rights?

> [!TIP]
> Standard user access is sufficient for the default install location. Administrator rights are only requested if you choose a system-wide install path during setup.

### 📂 Where does the build place its files?

> [!NOTE]
> By default, the installer uses the per-user program directory for the application and the user profile for configuration. No files are written to Windows system directories.

### 📶 Does the build collect telemetry?

> [!TIP]
> This standalone build does not include telemetry or usage reporting. All processing happens locally on the Windows host.

### 🐛 How do I report an issue?

> [!NOTE]
> Open a new issue on this repository with Windows version, build hash, and the reproduction steps. Include any installer log lines from `%TEMP%` if available.

# CAPRI

### Your personal desktop AI agent. Built for Night City, runs on your PC.

A local-first desktop agent with a cyberpunk soul. Capri sits on your machine, understands your intent, and executes: files, apps, browser, terminal, code. Plug in Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity or any other model backend and let it work.

[Release](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/releases/latest)
[Stars](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/stargazers)
[Platform](#installation)
[Build](#installation)
[License](LICENSE)

[**Download for Windows**](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/releases/latest)  |  [Features](#features)  |  [Architecture](#architecture)  |  [Roadmap](#roadmap)  |  [FAQ](#faq)

---

## What is Capri

Capri is an open desktop AI agent inspired by the aesthetics and ideas of the **Cyberpunk: Edgerunners** universe: a fast, sharp, always-on netrunner assistant that lives on your machine instead of a browser tab.

Most AI tools stop at a chat window. Capri goes further. It is an **agent runtime with a native desktop shell**: it receives a goal in natural language, plans the steps, calls tools on your system, observes the results, and iterates until the job is done. Think of it as your own Jarvis, only with a neon HUD and a much better soundtrack.

Capri is model-agnostic. It wraps the coding and reasoning agents you already use, such as **Claude Code**, **Codex** and **Antigravity**, behind one unified interface, so you can switch the brain without changing the body.

> Capri is an independent fan-inspired project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by CD PROJEKT RED, Studio Trigger, Netflix or Anthropic. See [Disclaimer](#disclaimer).

---

## Features

### Agent core

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **Natural language to action** | Describe the outcome you want. Capri decomposes it into a plan of tool calls and executes it step by step. |
| **Multi-backend brain** | Hot-swap between Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and other compatible agent backends from a single dropdown. |
| **Persistent memory** | Long-term context store so Capri remembers your projects, preferences and recurring workflows between sessions. |
| **Streaming reasoning view** | Watch the plan, tool calls and intermediate results in real time, with the ability to pause, edit or abort at any step. |
| **Task queue** | Fire off multiple jobs and let them run concurrently while you keep working. |

### System control

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **File operations** | Search, read, create, move, rename and batch-process files and folders with natural language. |
| **Terminal execution** | Run shell commands inside a sandboxed session with live output and a full audit log. |
| **App and window control** | Launch applications, focus windows, trigger hotkeys and automate repetitive UI flows. |
| **Browser automation** | Open pages, extract data, fill forms and run multi-step web tasks through a controlled browser context. |
| **Clipboard and screen context** | Optionally feed the current clipboard or a screen region to the agent as context. |

### Developer mode

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **Code agent integration** | Delegate refactors, bug hunts, test generation and repo analysis to your connected coding backend. |
| **Git awareness** | Diff, commit, branch and review changes with natural language, always behind a confirmation gate. |
| **Plugin and tool API** | Register custom tools with a simple JSON schema and let the agent call them. |
| **MCP compatibility** | Connect external tool servers through the Model Context Protocol. |

### Interface

- **Neon HUD overlay.** A lightweight always-on-top panel summoned with a global hotkey.
- **Command palette.** Keyboard-first input with fuzzy search over tools, history and saved workflows.
- **Voice input.** Push-to-talk dictation for hands-free commands.
- **Themes.** Built-in cyberpunk themes with adjustable glow, scanline and glitch intensity, plus a clean minimal mode.
- **Tray mode.** Runs quietly in the system tray with low idle footprint.

---

## Architecture

```
                 +--------------------------------------+
                 |             Capri Desktop            |
                 |   HUD overlay | Palette | Tray | Voice|
                 +------------------+-------------------+
                                    |
                           IPC / event bus
                                    |
                 +------------------v-------------------+
                 |             Agent Runtime            |
                 |  Planner -> Executor -> Observer     |
                 |  Memory store | Task queue | Policy  |
                 +---------+----------------+-----------+
                           |                |
              +------------v---+      +-----v--------------+
              | Backend Adapters|     |    Tool Layer      |
              | Claude Code     |     | FS | Shell | Web   |
              | Codex           |     | Apps | Git | MCP   |
              | Antigravity     |     | Custom plugins     |
              | Custom provider |     +--------------------+
              +-----------------+
```

**Design principles**

- **Local-first.** Your files, memory and logs stay on your machine. Only the prompts and context you choose to send leave it, and only to the backend you configured.
- **Adapter pattern.** Every model backend implements a small, typed interface, so adding a new provider is a matter of writing one adapter.
- **Human in the loop.** Destructive or irreversible actions pass through a configurable policy layer that requires explicit approval.
- **Observable by default.** Every plan, tool call and result is recorded in a structured, inspectable session log.

---

## Installation

> **Current platform support:** Windows 10 and Windows 11 (x64).
> **Current distribution:** portable ZIP build. No installer yet.

Capri ships as a self-contained portable archive. No installation, no registry changes, no admin rights required.

1. Open the [latest release](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/releases/latest).
2. Download `Capri-portable-x.y.z.zip`.
3. Extract the archive to any folder, for example `D:\Apps\Capri`.
4. Run `Capri.exe`.

On first launch, Capri walks you through connecting a backend.

Because the build is portable, you can keep it on a secondary drive or a USB stick. All settings, memory and logs are stored next to the executable, so moving or backing up Capri is just copying one folder.

**Updating.** Download the new ZIP and extract it over the old folder. Your `config.json`, `memory` and `tools` directories are preserved.

**Windows SmartScreen note.** New releases may not yet have an established reputation, so Windows can show a SmartScreen prompt. If you downloaded the archive from this repository's Releases page, choose **More info** and then **Run anyway**.

---

## Quick start

### 1. Connect a backend

Open **Settings > Backends** and pick the agent you want to power Capri:

| Backend | Setup |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | Sign in with your Anthropic account or provide an API key |
| Codex | Sign in with your OpenAI account or provide an API key |
| Antigravity | Sign in with your Google account |
| Custom | Point Capri at any compatible endpoint |

### 2. Summon Capri

Press the global hotkey (default `Ctrl + Alt + Space`) to open the HUD from anywhere.

### 3. Give it a job

```text
Sort my Downloads folder by file type, move installers into /Installers and delete duplicates older than 30 days.
```

```text
Open the project in D:\dev\netrunner, find why the tests in /auth are failing and propose a fix.
```

```text
Every morning at 9:00, open my dashboard, grab yesterday's numbers and put them in a note.
```

Capri shows its plan first. Approve it, edit it, or let it run in autonomous mode for trusted task types.

---

## Configuration

Capri reads its configuration from `config.json` located next to `Capri.exe`. Everything is also available in the Settings UI.

```json
{
  "backend": "claude-code",
  "hotkey": "Ctrl+Alt+Space",
  "theme": "edgerunner",
  "memory": {
    "enabled": true,
    "retentionDays": 90
  },
  "policy": {
    "requireApproval": ["delete", "shell", "git.push", "network.upload"],
    "autonomousMode": false
  },
  "sandbox": {
    "allowedPaths": ["C:\\Users\\you\\Projects", "C:\\Users\\you\\Downloads"]
  }
}
```

### Registering a custom tool

```json
{
  "name": "check_gpu_temp",
  "description": "Returns the current GPU temperature in Celsius",
  "command": "powershell -File tools/gpu_temp.ps1",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {},
    "required": []
  }
}
```

Drop the file into the `tools\` folder next to `Capri.exe` and restart Capri. The agent discovers it automatically.

---

## Security and privacy

- **Scoped access.** Capri can only touch directories you explicitly allow.
- **Approval gates.** Deletion, shell execution, pushes and uploads are gated by policy.
- **Audit log.** Every action is written to a local, append-only session log.
- **No telemetry by default.** Capri does not collect usage analytics unless you opt in.
- **Secrets stay local.** API keys and tokens are stored in the Windows Credential Manager, not in plain text.

Found a vulnerability? Please open a private security advisory instead of a public issue.

---

## Roadmap

- [x] Windows desktop shell with HUD overlay (portable)
- [x] Multi-backend adapter layer
- [x] File, shell and app tools
- [x] Portable ZIP build
- [x] Persistent memory
- [ ] Browser automation toolkit
- [ ] Voice input and wake word
- [ ] MCP server marketplace
- [ ] Workflow recorder and shareable macros
- [ ] Multi-agent mode with specialist sub-agents
- [ ] Scheduled and event-triggered tasks
- [ ] macOS and Linux builds
- [ ] Mobile companion for remote task dispatch

Have an idea? Open a [feature request](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/issues/new).

---

## FAQ

**Is Capri free?**
Capri itself is free and open source. Your chosen backend may require its own subscription or API key.

**Does it work offline?**
The desktop shell, tools and memory work offline. Reasoning requires a connected backend unless you point Capri at a local model endpoint.

**Is this the Capri from the show?**
No. Capri is an original project that borrows the mood of the cyberpunk genre and the Edgerunners universe. It has no official connection to the series.

**Can I use my own model?**
Yes. Implement the backend adapter interface or point Capri at any compatible endpoint.

**Will you support macOS and Linux?**
It is on the roadmap. Windows comes first.

---

## Contributing

Pull requests are welcome. For major changes, open an issue first so we can talk through the design.

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a branch: `git checkout -b feature/your-feature`
3. Commit your changes
4. Push and open a pull request

---

## Community

If Capri saves you time, a star helps other people find it. Bug reports, ideas and feedback live in [Issues](https://github.com/Outpostkrewhirl86/capri-ai/issues).

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
# STE80 Humanizer

[skills.sh installs](https://skills.sh/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer) [validate](https://github.com/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer/actions/workflows/validate.yml) [License: MIT](LICENSE)

Built by the team behind [Dodaios](https://github.com/Dodaios/Dodaios), the open-source assistant that runs your coding agents for you.

STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:

1. **The humanizer method.** Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's [Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing), in the catalog of [blader/humanizer](https://github.com/blader/humanizer).
2. **Karpathy's STE80 method.** Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.

**Before:**
> Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` should be carefully tuned.
>
> Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.

**After:**
> A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
>
> A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` to values that fit your application.

The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.

## Why two passes

Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md):

| Step | What is left |
|---|---|
| Original | Chatbot opener, dash, "not just X", "-ing" rider, "however", "could potentially", dramatic closer |
| After Pass 1 (tells) | "...the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, which keeps your application available. Misconfigured probes can cause cascading restarts, so parameters ... should be carefully tuned." Clean words, but heavy sentences. |
| After Pass 2 (STE80) | Short sentences, one idea each, active voice, the instruction apart from the description. |

## The method: what Karpathy said

On 2 October 2026, [Andrej Karpathy posted](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479) tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:

> Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.

The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.

[Simplified Technical English: overview. Document structure, anatomy of STE sentences, verb forms, dictionary entries, writing rule limits and history.](assets/ste100-overview.png)

*The STE overview graphic from [Karpathy's post](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479). Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.*

**ASD-STE100** (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:

- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most

**Why "80%"?** At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:

| STE rule | 100% (Strict mode) | 80% (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence length 20 / 25 | Hard limit | A few words over is fine |
| One idea per sentence | Always | Always |
| Active voice, simple tenses | Always | Always |
| Approved dictionary only | Yes | No, use the plain common word |
| "check", "test" as verbs | No | Yes |
| "may", "should" | No | Yes, for real uncertainty |
| Contractions | No | Yes, in casual text |
| Semicolons | No | No |

Karpathy's tip is about readability. It does not remove chatbot phrases, so Pass 1 does that first.

## How to read the skill

[SKILL.md](SKILL.md) has two numbered lists:

- **§1 to §26:** the AI tells (Pass 1).
- **S1 to S15:** the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).

Both lists are compact tables with a short example. Pass 2 says what changes between **80%** and **Strict**. The full entries, with **Watch for**, **Problem**, **Before** and **After**, are in [references/ai-tells.md](references/ai-tells.md) and [references/ste80-rules.md](references/ste80-rules.md). *Weak alone* means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.

## Installation

Once installed, the skill answers to `/ste80-humanizer`. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.

### Any agent (skills.sh)

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
```

Global install for one agent, or for all of them:

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'
```

Without `--global`, the skill goes into the current project only. The [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) from Vercel works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and many more agents.

### Claude Code plugin

```
/plugin marketplace add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
/plugin install ste80-humanizer@ste80-humanizer
```

### Claude.ai and Claude Desktop

Download this repo as a ZIP (Code → Download ZIP). Upload it in Settings → Capabilities → Skills.

## Usage

```
/ste80-humanizer

```

Or just ask:

```
This sounds like ChatGPT wrote it. Make it sound like a person.
Rewrite this README 80% of the way to ASD-STE100.
Explain how TLS handshakes work in STE.
Light touch: just remove the AI stuff from docs/intro.md.
Convert docs/runbook.md to strict STE.
Does this email sound like AI? Just tell me, don't rewrite it.
```

| Mode | When | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Humanize (default)** | Normal requests | Pass 1 fully, Pass 2 at 80%. Keeps your voice. |
| **Light** | "light touch", "just remove the AI stuff" | Pass 1, plus only the worst sentences from Pass 2. |
| **Strict STE** | "strict", "full STE", procedures, safety notes | Pass 1 and all of Pass 2 at 100%. |

**Match your voice.** Add a sample of your own writing. The skill then matches your sentence length, words and punctuation.

**Fidelity first.** The skill keeps every fact, keeps "may" as "may", keeps "40+" as "40+", adds nothing and flags contradictions in the source. In our tests, this was the clearest difference from a plain prompt (see Tests).

## Pass 1: the 26 AI tells

| # | Tell | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Staging instead of stating** ||||
| 1 | **Not X but Y** | It's not just a faster build tool, it's a new way to think. | The build tool caches each step. |
| 2 | **One-line closers** | ...No cold starts. No excuses. That's the power of the edge. | Latency dropped to 40 ms. |
| 3 | **Sayings that sound deep** | At its core, observability is the language of trust. | Shared dashboards show both teams the same data. |
| 4 | **Staged run-up** | Let's dive in. Here's what you need to know. | The API allows 100 requests per minute. |
| 5 | **Arguing with no one** | To be clear, I'm not saying microservices are bad... | We split the billing service out first. |
| **B. Rhythm by rule** ||||
| 6 | **Forced triads** | fast, intuitive, and powerful | loads in under a second |
| 7 | **Repeated openings** (*weak alone*) | It reads... It checks... It starts... | It reads the config and checks the schema. |
| 8 | **Dashes everywhere** | The migration — which took six weeks — is done. | The migration took six weeks and is done. |
| 9 | **Stacked qualifiers** (*weak alone*) | could potentially possibly cause | can break |
| 10 | **Hyphenated pairs** (*weak alone*) | The API is well-documented. | The API is well documented. |
| 11 | **Passive, missing subjects** (*weak alone*) | No account needed. | You do not need an account. |
| **C. Inflation and borrowed authority** ||||
| 12 | **Overused AI words** | leverages a robust caching layer, showcasing... | caches API responses on the device |
| 13 | **Inflated significance** | marks a pivotal moment in the project's journey | adds a CLI and drops Node 16 |
| 14 | **Vague association** | The outage was linked to the DNS change. | The DNS change caused the outage. |
| 15 | **Shallow -ing riders** | ..., highlighting its commitment to accessibility | (cut) |
| 16 | **Sales language** | our groundbreaking, world-class editor | The editor runs inside VS Code. |
| 17 | **Borrowed authority** | Experts agree... featured in TechCrunch, Wired... | It was on the front page of Hacker News in May. |
| 18 | **Avoiding is / has** | serves as the central hub and boasts 40 options | holds the settings. It has 40 options. |
| **D. Formatting by rule** ||||
| 19 | **Bold as decoration** | **Performance:** Performance has been improved. | The release makes pages load faster. |
| 20 | **Decorative headings** | ## 🚀 Getting Started With The CLI → | ## Install the CLI |
| 21 | **Curly quotes** (*weak alone*) | “true” | "true" |
| **E. Leftovers from the chat and the draft** ||||
| 22 | **Chatbot residue** | Great question! ... I hope this helps! | (cut the wrapper) |
| 23 | **Knowledge-limit hedges** | While details are limited, it was likely created around 2015. | The sources do not say. |
| 24 | **Heading repeated** | ## Security / Security is important. | (cut the line) |
| 25 | **Writing about the document** | This function was added to replace the old approach... | This function looks up users in a hash map. |
| **F. Writing for the wrong reader** ||||
| 26 | **Re-explaining what the reader knows** | A reply that walks through the whole diagnosis first | Agreed. I'll switch the job to UTC. |

## Pass 2: the 15 STE80 rules

| # | Rule | 80% vs Strict |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | One idea per sentence | 80% allows two linked facts with "and" or "because" |
| S2 | Short sentences: 20 words (instructions), 25 (descriptions) | 80% allows a small overrun |
| S3 | Condition first: "If X, do Y." | Same |
| S4 | Do not drop words ("the", "a", "that") | 80% allows fragments in tables and headings |
| S5 | Lists for steps and complex content | Same |
| S6 | Active voice | Same |
| S7 | Simple tenses only | Same |
| S8 | Verbs, not nouns, no "-ing" chains | Strict: "check" and "test" are nouns |
| S9 | Honest moda

# 🎨 CorelDraw Desktop 2026: Standalone Offline Build for Windows 11

## 📦 Intro

This repository packages a standalone offline Windows x64 distribution intended for the CorelDraw Desktop workflow, provided as a self-contained setup for Windows 10 and 11. The distribution bundles the runtime, the asset libraries, and the configuration defaults required to run the vector design workflow on a clean host without relying on a live CDN at first launch. It is maintained as a reproducible deployment artifact rather than a vendor-issued release.

The build targets operators who need deterministic installs: air-gapped design workstations, lab machines with restricted outbound connectivity, and deployment pipelines that require a pinned artifact hash. Because the package resolves all dependencies at build time, it can be mirrored internally and replayed across identical machines without drift. This makes the standalone setup useful wherever bandwidth is limited or reproducibility is a hard requirement.

A single `CorelDraw Desktop on Windows` deployment covers both portable and installed modes, so the same offline bundle can serve a shared workstation and a per-user install without a second download. The distribution ships the vector graphics and layout modules along with format import/export handlers for the common interchange formats used in print and web design workflows.

## 01 · ⬇️ Download

## 02 · ✨ Features

**🎯 Vector Drafting**

Precision node and curve editing for print and web layout work.

**🖼️ Raster Import**

Brings in common bitmap formats alongside vector objects on the canvas.

**📐 Page Layout**

Multi-page document handling with bleed, margin, and grid guides.

**🎨 Color Management**

ICC profile handling and spot color mapping for consistent output.

**💾 Format Export**

Vector and raster export paths tuned for downstream print pipelines.

**📦 Portable Mode**

Runs from a self-contained folder without touching system directories.

## 03 · ⚙️ How it works

The installer delivers the application binaries into the per-user program directory and stages shared asset libraries alongside them. Format handler modules and color profile data land in the same tree so the runtime can resolve them without a system-wide installer step. No components are written into `C:\Windows` or other protected system locations.

On first launch the build writes a configuration profile into the user profile under the local application data path. It registers file associations through the per-user registry hive rather than the machine hive, so a standard user account can complete the setup without elevation. Default workspace, palette, and template selections are copied into the profile on this first run.

At runtime the build operates fully offline. There is no background updater, no license phone-home, and no telemetry endpoint contacted during normal use. Updates are delivered as a newer versioned offline bundle; running it over an existing install preserves the user profile, workspaces, and saved documents.

Integration with the host is limited to the per-user registry, shell file associations, and the Start menu shortcuts created during install. The build coexists with other installations of similar software because it does not claim system-wide file handler ownership by default. External dependencies are resolved from the bundled runtime rather than from the host.

## 04 · 🧩 Compatibility

The build targets Windows 10 and Windows 11 on x64 only. Both Home and Pro editions are supported, and the current Windows feature update channel is assumed. 32-bit and ARM64 targets are out of scope for this distribution.

PowerShell 5.1 is the minimum shell baseline for the verification scripts, with PowerShell 7 preferred for the newer cmdlets used during checksum validation. The installer itself does not require PowerShell at runtime; the scripts are provided for operators who want to verify the artifact before deployment.

The build runs on modest hardware: an x64 CPU from the last several generations, a few gigabytes of available RAM for typical documents, and several gigabytes of free disk for the program directory plus working assets. Comfortable on workstations with additional RAM when handling large multi-page layouts.

Coexistence is handled by keeping everything inside the per-user profile and program directory. Portable mode runs from an extracted folder without registering file associations, which is useful when the build is staged on a shared drive. Installed mode registers associations in the current user's hive, so it does not overwrite machine-wide handler registrations from other installations.

## 05 · 🔧 Requirements

| Component | Supported | Preferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OS | Windows 10 | Windows 11 |

# Gemini Config Checker

Find proxy configs that actually get you into **Google AI Studio and Gemini**, by testing each one the way a person would: in a
*signed-in* browser, through the route you will really use.

> **Version 0.1.0, early pre-release.** It works end to end on Windows (the only platform it has been run on so far). The macOS,
> Linux and Android builds come from the CI pipeline and have not been exercised on real devices yet. Please report what you find.

## Two modes, one switch

The big **Simple / Advanced** switch in the header decides what is tested. The route diagram under the title morphs to show it.

| | **Simple** | **Advanced** |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | *Which of my configs work?* | *Which free configs work through my config?* |
| Route | you → **config** → AI Studio / Gemini | you → **base config** → **free config** → AI Studio / Gemini |
| You provide | your configs (links, a subscription URL or base64), or pick a ready-made free list | one working base config, plus a free list or pasted configs |
| Anti-DPI profile is applied to | every config under test (each one connects from your machine) | the base config's first hop (free configs run inside its tunnel) |
| Typical use | check a pile of configs you already have; test a config before you rely on it | your Cloudflare config works, but you need a *different exit* that Google accepts |
| Export | links, base64, a full Xray config of one config | links, base64, a chain Xray config (`base → free`) |

1. Download `gemini-config-checker_ _android_arm64.apk` on the phone.

3. Launch the app. A persistent notification ("Scanner engine is running") is expected: the engine runs as a foreground service so long scans survive the screen turning off. Use its **Stop** action to quit the engine.
4. The APK runs the **connectivity-only** mode (see [Settings reference](#7-settings-reference)). Android does not let apps drive a signed-in Chromium, so the region cannot be verified there.

The UI has **no authentication**: keep it on localhost, or tunnel it (`ssh -L 8787:localhost:8787 your-server`) instead of exposing it.

## User guide

### 1. First start
The window has three tabs: **Scan** (what to test and how), **Results** (live list, filters, copy buttons) and **Export**.
The header holds the **Simple / Advanced** switch, the scan status, and a light/dark theme button. Everything you type is remembered on this
device when "remember" is ticked (untick it on a shared computer).

### 2. Pick a mode
* Use **Simple** when you already have configs and want to know which ones work, or to verify the config you are about to rely on.
* Use **Advanced** when your Cloudflare config connects fine but Google blocks its exit: free configs chained behind it give you other exits.
* You can flip the switch at any time. Results keep the mode of the scan that produced them; Export and the copy buttons follow that.

### 3. Sign in with Google (region check)
The region check opens AI Studio and Gemini as *you*. Click **Sign in with Google** once:
1. A Chrome / Edge / Brave window opens in a **separate profile** that only this app uses. Sign in normally. The app never sees your password.
2. When sign-in is detected the window closes by itself and the card turns to "Google account connected". The sign-in is remembered for next time.
3. Prefer a **secondary account**: requests come from many IPs, so Google may show a "suspicious sign-in" notice.
4. **Remove account from app** deletes only that private profile. It never touches your everyday browser or accounts.

No browser installed, or on Android? Switch the *check type* (Settings) to **connectivity only**: no sign-in or browser needed.

### 4. Simple mode, step by step
1. Paste your configs into the box, one per line: `vless://`, `vmess://`, `trojan://`, `ss://`. A subscription URL (`https://…`) or base64 text also works.
   Leave the box empty to test a ready-made free list instead (pick one below).
2. Keep **Anti-DPI** on if you are inside a network where plain Cloudflare configs do not connect (see [section 6](#6-the-anti-dpi-profile)).
3. Sign in (region check) or choose connectivity only.
4. Press **Start scan** (or `Ctrl`+`Enter`). Watch the **Results** tab fill in.

### 5. Advanced mode, step by step
1. **Base config**: a config that works for you and does *not* get the region wall on AI Studio. Paste a share link, or a full xray JSON, even a multi-hop chain
   (for example an exit that already dials through a Cloudflare worker). This is the route every free config will be chained behind.
2. **Anti-DPI**: applied to the base config's first hop, the connection that leaves your machine.
3. **Source**: choose a ready-made list (`verified` is recommended) or paste free configs yourself. `custom` accepts any subscription URL.
4. Settings, sign-in, **Start scan**. Before testing the free configs, the app tests your base config first and stops with a clear message if the base itself cannot reach Google.

### 6. The anti-DPI profile
Inside Iran, plain Cloudflare configs mostly connect only with the settings below
([recipe by patterniha / PattN](https://t.me/MatinSenPaii/5469)). The values can change, so every one is editable; **Suggested values** restores the defaults.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Finalmask (JSON) | two `fragment` masks: `tlshello` with `lengths [0,104,1]`, then `1-1` with `lengths [114,1]` | splits the TLS ClientHello so filters cannot read the server name |
| Fingerprint | `unsafe` | native Go TLS instead of a browser imitation, so the cipher list below applies |
| ALPN | `http/1.1` | |
| Cipher suites | the 13-suite list from the recipe | |
| Clean IP | empty | replaces the connection address (the old domain stays as SNI and Host) |

* **Read from config**: if the config you pasted already carries these values (`finalmask`, `cipherSuites`, `alpn` in JSON, or `fm`, `ciphers`, `alpn`, `fp` link parameters), this button copies them into the form.
* Stock xray-core only supports one `length`/`delay` per fragment mask, while the recipe uses per-segment `lengths`/`delays` (a PattN fork feature). The app runs the same
  fragmenting algorithm in a small local forwarder in front of the connection. Only `fragment` masks are supported; other mask types are rejected with a clear message.
* Switch the profile off outside filtered networks; it only adds latency there.

### 7. Settings reference
| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Check type | Region with signed-in browser | **Region**: opens AI Studio and Gemini and reads Google's verdict (accurate, 20–40 s per config). **Connectivity only**: just proves the route reaches Google and measures latency (fast, no sign-in, but the region is *not* checked) |
| "Healthy" means | AI Studio **and** Gemini | Require both, only AI Studio, or only Gemini |
| Max configs | 60 | How many configs to test (the list is shuffled first) |
| Simultaneous browser checks | 4 | Each uses about 200 MB of RAM; lower it on small machines |
| Simultaneous connectivity tests | 20 | The cheap first stage that drops dead configs before the browser stage |
| Connectivity timeout | 10 s | Raise it on slow links |
| Remember | on | Stores confi

4. Settings, sign-in, **Start scan**. Before testing the free configs, the app tests your base config first and stops with a clear message if the base itself cannot reach Google.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Finalmask (JSON) | two `fragment` masks: `tlshello` with `lengths [0,104,1]`, then `1-1` with `lengths [114,1]` | splits the TLS ClientHello so filters cannot read the server name |
| Fingerprint | `unsafe` | native Go TLS instead of a browser imitation, so the cipher list below applies |
| ALPN | `http/1.1` | |
| Cipher suites | the 13-suite list from the recipe | |
| Clean IP | empty | replaces the connection address (the old domain stays as SNI and Host) |

* Stock xray-core only supports one `length`/`delay` per fragment mask, while the recipe uses per-segment `lengths`/`delays` (a PattN fork feature). The app runs the same
  fragmenting algorithm in a small local forwarder in front of the connection. Only `fragment` masks are supported; other mask types are rejected with a clear message.
* Switch the profile off outside filtered networks; it only adds latency there.

### 7. Settings reference

| Check type | Region with signed-in browser | **Region**: opens AI Studio and Gemini and reads Google's verdict (accurate, 20–40 s per config). **Connectivity only**: just proves the route reaches Google and measures latency (fast, no sign-in, but the region is *not* checked) |
| "Healthy" means | AI Studio **and** Gemini | Require both, only AI Studio, or only Gemini |
| Max configs | 60 | How many configs to test (the list is shuffled first) |
| Simultaneous browser checks | 4 | Each uses about 200 MB of RAM; lower it on small machines |
| Simultaneous connectivity tests | 20 | The cheap first stage that drops dead configs before the browser stage |
| Connectivity timeout | 10 s | Raise it on slow links |

## Features

### Chat or Terminal

Run any agent in Chat UI or as the raw CLI, and move a conversation between the two without losing context.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/agents/native-chat)

### Orchestrate Agents

Hand a big task to one agent. It splits the work, starts worker agents in their own workspaces, and brings their results back to you.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/orchestration)

### Run Anywhere

Pair a Remote Orca Server, work on any SSH host, or give a worktree its own cloud VM. Your agents keep running when your laptop sleeps.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/ways-to-run)

### Mobile App

Pair Orca with the mobile app to get pinged when an agent needs you, reply in chat, and keep work moving on any of your machines when you are away from your desk.

[iOS App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/orca-ide/id6766130217) · [Android APK](https://orca.dev/download/android) · [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/mobile)

### Review AI Output

Review diffs, leave notes on exact changed lines, and send focused feedback back to an agent.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/annotate-ai-diff)

### Git Integration

Draft commit messages and pull requests from the diff, then send failing checks or PR review comments back to an agent to fix.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/commit-push)

### Parallel Worktrees

Quickly split tasks into isolated environments, so multiple agents can work side by side without interfering with each other.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/model/worktrees)

### Design Mode

Click any element in Orca's browser to copy its HTML, styles, and selector, then paste it into your agent's chat.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/browser/design-mode)

### GitHub & Linear, Native

See your GitHub and Linear tasks in one place, and start a workspace for each when you're ready to build.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/linear)

### Orca CLI

Anything you can do in Orca, your agents can do too: create worktrees, start workers, drive the browser and desktop apps, and schedule automations, all from the command line.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/overview)

### Plugins

Themes, editors, languages, and panels from the community, installed in a click.

[Browse plugins →](https://orca.dev/plugins)

### Split Anything

Put agents, terminals, browsers, and diffs side by side in split panes shaped to the task.

[Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/model/tabs-panes-splits)

- **[Usage & Accounts](https://orca.dev/docs/agents/usage-tracking)**: see how much of your agent limits you've used and when they reset, and switch accounts without logging out.

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
**Ballast runs [k6](https://k6.io) load tests as a service, for several projects
at once.** A user picks a project, a scenario and a target environment, queues a
run, and reads the results in plain words. No infrastructure code, and no way to
aim load at a server you do not own.

**Try it at [myballast.pro](https://myballast.pro)**: free during the beta, sign in
with GitHub or Google. Or [run it yourself](#self-hosting).

## How it works

- **Visual scenario builder**: draw a test on a canvas (requests, variables,
  conditions, loops, assertions), or write a k6 script. Ballast generates the
  same script from the same graph, byte for byte.
- **Import** what you already have: OpenAPI, Postman collections, cURL and HAR.
  Secrets found in a file are never copied.
- **Safe by design**: load is only ever sent to environments whose ownership
  has been verified; the load generator runs in an isolated container with no
  route of its own to the network; hard limits on virtual users and duration.
- **Results you can read**: thresholds, p95/p99, error rate, throughput, and
  every number explained.

## Status

Ballast is in public beta and under active development. The hosted version at
myballast.pro is free during the beta; a paid plan will come later, and
self-hosting stays free. The API and the database schema can still change
between versions.

## Limits

- **200 virtual users and one hour per run.** These are constants in the code, not
  settings: Ballast is built for realistic multi-step API scenarios, not for
  simulating a million users.
- **One region.** Load leaves from Ballast's own servers.
- **HTTP and HTTPS only.**
- **Targets must be reachable from the internet** and their ownership proved
  before any run.
- **No run comparison or trends yet**: each run has its own verdict.
- **A young project**, built by one person.

## Self-hosting

Run all of Ballast on one machine, from images. You need Docker (with Compose)
and `openssl`, nothing else.

```bash
make selfhost
```

The first run writes `.env.selfhost` with generated passwords and keys, and
stops short of letting anyone in: Ballast stores no password, so people sign in
with GitHub or Google, and that needs an OAuth app of your own. Create one at
https://github.com/settings/developers with

- Homepage URL: `http://localhost:3000`
- Authorization callback URL: `http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`

put its client ID and secret in `.env.selfhost`, and run `make selfhost` again.
Ballast is on http://localhost:3000; the first sign-in creates your
organization. `make selfhost-logs` follows it, `make selfhost-down` stops it and
keeps the data.

What to know before you rely on it:

- **Only targets reachable from the internet can be tested.** A target is
  verified by reading a challenge file from it, and the verifier refuses
  private, loopback and link-local addresses, with no setting to allow them.
  A staging server on your own network cannot be verified.
- **The worker holds the Docker socket**, which gives it what root has on the
  host: it starts each run's generator and proxy through it. Run it on a
  machine you dedicate to Ballast.
- **No TLS.** The front end is published on `127.0.0.1` only. To open it to
  anyone else, put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front, and set
  `BALLAST_PUBLIC_URL` and `BALLAST_WEB_URL` to its `https` address (and the
  OAuth app's URLs with them).
- **Stopping drains.** `make selfhost-down` lets a run in progress finish,
  up to an hour and six minutes, rather than cut a measurement in half.
- **One worker, three runs at a time**, two per organization. More wait in the
  queue.
- Keep `BALLAST_SECRET_KEY` with your database backups: without it, the
  secrets stored in the database cannot be read.

The sections below are for working on Ballast itself.

## Prerequisites

- Go 1.23
- Docker (Postgres, the k6 generators, and the API documentation tools)
- Node.js 22 and npm (the front end)

## Getting started

```bash
cp .env.example .env      # then fill in the GitHub OAuth app, see below
make up && make migrate
make seed                 # once: a development organization, scenario and environment
make dev                  # API on :8080, worker, front end on :3000
```

`make down` stops everything, wherever it was started.

### Signing in

Ballast stores no password: people sign in with GitHub or Google. For local
development, create a GitHub OAuth app at https://github.com/settings/developers:

- Homepage URL: `http://localhost:3000`
- Authorization callback URL: `http://localhost:8080/auth/github/callback`

and put its client ID and secret in `.env`. Never in `.env.example`, which is
committed.

The first sign-in creates an organization, with a first project its user
administers. `make worker` only takes runs from `BALLAST_WORKER_ORG_ID` (the
seeded organization by default); a worker with that variable empty serves every organization.

## Commands

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `make dev` | Postgres, migrations, then the API, the worker and the front end together |
| `make api` / `make worker` / `make web` | One process at a time |
| `make stop` / `make down` | Stop the processes / and Postgres |
| `make migrate` | Apply the database migrations |
| `make sqlc` | Regenerate the Go code from `internal/adapter/postgres/queries` |
| `make test` | Unit tests, including the API contract check |
| `make test-int` | Integration tests, needs `make up` and Docker |
| `make lint` / `make web-lint` | Go / front-end linters |
| `make api-docs` | Swagger UI on http://localhost:8081 |
| `make api-lint` | Validate the OpenAPI spec |

## API

The contract is `docs/api/openapi.yaml`, OpenAPI 3.1, written by hand.

```bash
make api-docs   # browse it in Swagger UI on http://localhost:8081
make api-lint   # validate it
```

Every route except the health check and the sign-in flow needs the
`ballast_session` cookie, which signing in sets. It is `HttpOnly`, so Swagger
UI's "Try it out" cannot send it; use the front end, or `curl` with the cookie
copied from the browser's developer tools.

**Keeping it true.** Any change that adds, modifies or removes an endpoint
updates `openapi.yaml` in the same change. `make test` enforces the part a
machine can check: `internal/adapter/http/openapi_test.go` fails when a route
registered in `internal/adapter/http/router.go` is missing from the spec, when
a documented route no longer exists, or when a route is public on one side and
behind a session on the other. Request and response shapes come from
`internal/adapter/http/dto/`.

## Front end

```bash
cd web && npm ci
npm run lint
npm run typecheck   # runs `next typegen` first: the route types are generated
npm test
```

## Responsible use

Ballast is a load-testing tool. It only sends load to targets whose ownership
has been proven (a challenge file served from the target's own origin), and a
run against an environment that has not been verified is refused. Do not use it
to attack systems you do not own or operate.

## Security

Please do not open a public issue for a vulnerability. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
